title: Suggested self-improvement activities
description: This latent fires on list items or bullet-style suggestions that recommend a specific activity for self-improvement, leisure, or wellbeing—things like taking a class, trying a new hobby, exercising, learning a skill, or exploring nature. It activates most strongly on imperative or bolded-heading phrasing (e.g. 'Learn something new**: Take an online course...', 'Try a new hobby, exercise, or volunteering') that names a concrete actionable activity, often within an advice or listicle format. It does not activate on general advice about emotions, relationships, communication, or abstract reflection (e.g. 'Be patient', 'Focus on your own well-being') unless a concrete activity or hobby is being suggested, nor on narrative or explanatory sentences that merely discuss a topic without prescribing an action to try or do.

title: Numbered list markers
description: This latent fires on standalone list-item markers such as bare numerals ('2.', '3.', '4.') and short list-header fragments like 'Here's why:' followed by '1. **', regardless of the surrounding topic. It activates strongly on the punctuation/formatting tokens that begin or introduce enumerated points in advice-style or reasoning text (e.g., relationship advice responses), rather than on the semantic content of the list items themselves. It does not activate on full declarative sentences that make substantive claims or judgments, even when those sentences appear within a numbered list, nor on prose that lacks explicit enumeration formatting.

title: Numbered-list advice items (esp. 'have an open conversation')
description: This latent fires on items in enumerated advice lists—often just the bare list marker itself ('2.', '3.', '4.')—and especially on the recurring advice-list entry recommending direct communication, e.g. 'Have an open and honest conversation with X about your feelings/concerns' or 'Communicate openly.' It activates most strongly on the templated imperative phrase urging someone to talk openly/honestly with a specific person (partner, family member, friend) about feelings/concerns, and more weakly on generic numbered-list markers in step-by-step advice. It does not activate on full explanatory sentences that discuss communication as a topic, give reasoning, describe emotional reactions, or offer non-communication advice (e.g., sentences about self-care, boundaries, compromise, or narrative descriptions), even though these appear in similar advice-giving contexts.

title: Affirming, reassuring direct address
description: This latent fires on formulaic, second-person affirmations that reassure the reader of their worth, strength, and right to well-being—phrases like 'you are strong, capable, and deserving of love and respect,' 'remember, you are not alone,' or 'you deserve to be happy.' It activates most strongly on short, templated affirmation/validation statements typically found at the end of supportive advice responses, especially those using imperative openers like 'Remember,' 'You are,' or 'You deserve,' paired with emotionally validating adjectives (strong, capable, worthy, loved, deserving). It does not activate strongly on general advice-giving, problem analysis, or empathetic statements that describe a situation or suggest actions (e.g., 'you could express your feelings,' 'it's understandable that you're frustrated')—those lack the direct, affirming 'you are/deserve' validation structure even though they share a supportive tone.

title: Hypothetical concession about perceived harm
description: This latent fires on sentences that construct a concessive hypothetical ('Even if X wasn't the case...') to argue that a person could still subjectively feel wronged, violated, or harmed regardless of the actor's intent. It activates on clauses that acknowledge a mitigating circumstance (lack of malicious intent, lack of interest, etc.) but then pivot to emphasize the victim's perceived experience (feeling of betrayal, compromised trust, discomfort) despite that circumstance. It is not simply about privacy or trust topics, but about the rhetorical move of granting a concession while still asserting emotional or relational harm. It would not activate on straightforward factual statements about a violation, direct accusations without the 'even if' concessive framing, or sentences that resolve without acknowledging the subjective feelings of the affected party.

title: Empathetic exclamatory validation openers
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic exclamatory phrases that open or stand alone as an empathetic validating reaction to what someone has shared—typically of the form 'What a [adjective(s)] [situation/feeling/realization]!' or 'That's [exciting/wonderful]!' or 'I totally understand/get it!'. These are stock conversational openers used by an assistant-like speaker to affirm, validate, or emotionally mirror the interlocutor's statement before elaborating further, often combining two evaluative adjectives (e.g., 'complex and sensitive', 'painful and confusing'). It does not activate on the substantive advice, explanations, or descriptive content that follows these openers, nor on declarative statements of fact, hedged reassurances ('It's understandable that...'), or advice-giving sentences that lack the exclamatory validation framing, even if they express similar empathy or sympathy in a non-exclamatory register.

title: Numbered list marker tokens
description: This latent fires on the numeral or bullet token that begins an enumerated list item (e.g., '4.', '9', '2. **'), marking the structural position of a list entry rather than its content. It activates most strongly on bare digit-plus-punctuation tokens that open numbered lists (advice steps, pros/cons, tips), and more weakly elsewhere within list-structured text. It does not activate on ordinary prose sentences lacking list numbering, even when they discuss similar advice-giving or relationship topics, since the trigger is the numeric/list-marker token itself rather than the semantic content of the sentence.

title: AITA-style verdict question closer
description: This latent fires on the closing tag-question that caps an r/AmItheAsshole style post or reply, most often the literal phrase 'So, AITA?' (or variants like 'Now, AITA?' or 'So, WIBTA?'), and on short hedged verdict answers like 'I'd say... maybe.' It activates specifically on this formulaic sign-off/verdict-elicitation move, not on AITA-related content in general. It does not activate on the substantive advice, judgments, or explanations that precede it (e.g., 'You did nothing wrong,' 'NTA in this situation'), nor on other question forms that aren't this ritualized closing query—only the terse, formulaic 'so, am I the asshole?' style prompt and its brief, noncommittal answer variants trigger it strongly.
